title: Everyone Thinks Everyone Else Drinks More
text:
In the early 1990s, Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller at Princeton University asked undergraduates two simple questions: how comfortable they personally felt with the drinking habits on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average Princeton student felt.

The students consistently believed that the average student was much more comfortable with heavy drinking than they themselves were. Since the average of their own answers was the actual average student, most of them were wrong about their peers. Each person privately had doubts but assumed everyone else was at ease. This is what social psychologists call pluralistic ignorance: a group in which most members privately reject a norm while wrongly believing that most others accept it.

The researchers followed some students over a semester and found that the misperception had consequences. Male students, in particular, gradually shifted their own attitudes toward what they believed the norm to be. Students who felt that they were out of step with their peers also reported feeling more alienated from the university.

Prentice and Miller suggested that norms like campus drinking can persist because everyone acts according to what they think others want, even when few actually want it.
lesson: A group's apparent consensus may be a shared misunderstanding. If you privately doubt a team norm, say so; others may have been waiting for someone to speak.
source: Prentice, D. A., and Miller, D. T. (1993). Pluralistic ignorance and alcohol use on campus: Some consequences of misperceiving the social norm. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(2), 243-256.
